title: The camera with no film
hook: Your own engineer has built a camera with no film. Film is how you make your money. What do you do?

profit.label: Profit
profit.hint: Money the film business makes today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Kodak is for what comes next

intro.text: Rochester, New York, 1975. You run Kodak, and about 9 in every 10 rolls of film sold in America are yours. You earn from every holiday photo: from the film, the chemicals and the paper it is printed on. Your job is to keep it that way.

lab.text: In December 1975, an engineer in your lab, Steve Sasson, finishes a strange box. It weighs 8 pounds and takes 23 seconds to save one blurry black-and-white picture onto a cassette tape. You need a TV to see the picture, and there is no film anywhere inside it.

d1.title: The camera with no film
d1.setup: Today the camera is slow and blurry, and nobody would buy it. But if it keeps getting better, one day people will not need film, and film is where most of your money comes from.
d1.question: What do you do with the digital camera?
d1.advisor: Film pays every salary in this building. But whoever learns this first may own photography one day.

options.label: Patent it and keep it in the lab. Film pays the bills, and this isn't ready.
options.outcome: Kodak patents the camera, but the managers who see it aren't convinced. Its inventor later remembers them doubting that anyone would want to look at their pictures on a TV. No digital camera goes on sale.
options.why: Protecting your best business felt safe. But a new technology that looks worse at first can still replace you, and every year you wait, someone else learns it first.
options.better: Give digital a small team of its own that is allowed to compete with film, and pay for it from film profits.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you protected film instead of learning digital.

options.label: Start small: a few engineers, kept apart from film and free to compete with it.
options.outcome: You give the inventor a small team and a building away from the film offices. Film keeps paying the bills, while the team quietly learns about sensors, memory and screens.
options.why: You kept the money machine running while you learned how the next one might work. A separate team has room to grow without being held back by the business it may one day replace.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you gave digital its own room to grow, paid for by film.

options.label: Go big: put it on sale soon and be first, even though it's slow and costly to make.
options.outcome: You rush a camera into stores. It is bulky and slow, and you need a TV to see anything. Almost nobody buys it, and the loss shows up in your next yearly report.
options.why: The idea was right, but the market was not ready. In 1975 almost nobody had a screen worth looking at photos on, so being first did little if customers could not use what you sold.
options.better: Keep building it in a separate team, and launch when screens and memory are ready.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you were right about digital, but far too early.

text.text: August 1981. Sony shows the Mavica, a camera that saves pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. It isn't digital yet, but it needs no film, and it carries Sony's name, not yours.

August 1981. Sony shows the Mavica, a camera that saves pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. Your own digital team isn't surprised, because they have been working on the same idea for six years.
August 1981. Sony shows the Mavica, a camera that saves pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. Your own early camera flopped, but now Sony is making the same idea look exciting.

d2.title: Sony's filmless camera
d2.setup: One of your biggest photo-printing customers calls to ask whether they should be worried. Your investors want an answer too, and film still brings in most of your money.
d2.question: How do you respond to Sony?
d2.advisor: If we move too fast, we may hurt film. If we move too slowly, we may lose time we cannot get back.

options.label: Reassure customers and investors: film is far sharper, and Sony's camera isn't even digital.
options.outcome: Investors relax, and film keeps selling. But inside Kodak, everyone hears the message that digital is not where careers are made, and your best young engineers start looking at other jobs.
options.why: Early versions of a new technology are often worse. Comparing today's quality can hide the bigger question: how quickly is it getting better?
options.better: Accept that digital is coming, and start moving money and people toward it while film is still strong.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you judged digital by how good it was, not by how fast it was improving.

options.label: Order a careful study first: how many years before this beats film? It will take months.

outcome.text: Your head of market research reports back that digital could replace film, but Kodak has about ten years to get ready. Your digital team keeps working, but you keep its budget small, so it moves slowly.
Your head of market research reports back that digital could replace film, but Kodak has about ten years to get ready. Kodak does very little with those years.

options.why: The study was right about the danger. The mistake was treating ten years as permission to wait, because a deadline only helps if you start moving long before it.
options.better: Use the ten years to move money and people into digital now, not in year nine.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you saw the danger clearly, but treated the time you had as comfort, not a deadline.

options.label: Start moving film profits into digital now. Profits will fall, and investors will complain.

outcome.text: You take the 1975 camera out of the cupboard and put its inventor in charge. You are six years late, but Kodak still has the money, the patents and the name to catch up.
You announce that a bigger share of film profits will pay for digital every year. Investors grumble about lower profits, but your engineers stop looking for other jobs.

options.why: You used money from the old business to pay for the new one while you still could, which is the move most leading companies make too late.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you used today's profits to pay for tomorrow's business.

text.text: It is 2001, twenty years after you began paying for digital out of film profits. Kodak cameras are among the best sellers in America, and people are starting to put their photos online. You have just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload their pictures.

It is 2001. For twenty years Kodak called digital a toy, and now digital cameras are selling fast while film sales start to fall. Kodak is racing to catch up, and you have just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload their pictures.

It is 2001. The small digital team you started in 1975 is now a real business, and Kodak cameras sell well. But film still earns most of your money, and film sales have started to fall. You have just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload their pictures.

It is 2001. Twenty years on, digital cameras are finally selling, and your EasyShare cameras have made Kodak number two in the US. But film still earns most of your money, and film sales have started to fall. You have just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload their pictures.

d3.title: The photo website
d3.setup: Soon millions of people will keep their photos online. But Kodak earns its money when photos are printed, on Kodak paper, with Kodak chemicals.
d3.question: What is Ofoto for?
d3.advisor: Prints pay us today. Sharing might pay us one day. Nobody can tell us which one matters more.

options.label: Use it to sell prints. People upload photos, then order copies from you.
options.outcome: Renamed Kodak Gallery, the site grows until more than 60 million people use it. But people must keep buying from Kodak to keep their accounts, or their photos can be deleted.
options.why: You built the website around your old way of earning instead of the new way people wanted to use photos. People were moving away from printing memories and toward sharing them.
options.better: Make it a free place to share photos with friends, and earn from the people who use it, not from paper.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you built for your old income instead of your customers' new habit.

options.label: Make it free and easy to share photos with friends, and work out how to earn later.
options.outcome: Uploads are free, albums are easy to share, and friends comment on each other's photos. Within a few years, Kodak owns the place where families keep their pictures, just as phones start taking good ones.
options.why: You followed your customers' new habit, sharing, even though it hurt print sales. Owning the place people visit every day is worth more than owning the paper.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you followed your customers' new habit instead of your old income.

options.label: Close the website and put everything into making the best digital cameras.
options.outcome: Kodak cameras fly off the shelves, and the name looks modern again. But every rival is selling cameras too, and prices fall every year.
options.why: Cameras were a real business, but a crowded one with thin profits. You gave up the part of digital that people come back to every day.
options.better: Keep the website and make it about sharing, because that is where people would spend their time.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you chose selling cameras over owning the place where people's photos live.

text.text: It is 2007. Film is falling fast across the industry, but your digital businesses are growing fast enough to carry Kodak. You still have a strong hand, so the next choice matters.
It is 2007. Film is falling fast, but millions of families keep their photos on your free website, so the Kodak name is part of their lives online. Now you need a business that earns real money.
It is 2007. Film is falling fast, camera prices drop every year, and phones take better pictures each year. Your camera business is busy, but it barely earns anything.
It is 2007. Film is falling fast. Kodak has closed factories and cut thousands of jobs, and your photo website earns money mainly when people buy prints. Film is not coming back.

d4.title: The last chance
d4.setup: You still have skilled chemists, valuable patents, factories and one of the best-known names in the world. But you can afford one big bet, and only one.
d4.question: Where do you bet the company's future?
d4.advisor: Our name still sells. The question is whether people still want the things it sells.

options.label: Become the leading digital camera maker. Your name sells, though prices keep falling.
options.outcome: You win shelf space, then lose money on every price cut. Within a few years, the phone in everyone's pocket takes good enough pictures, and the camera market starts to shrink.
options.why: You picked a market where prices only go down, while a bigger threat, the phone, was already arriving.
options.better: Use what Kodak is best at, chemistry and materials, to enter new markets that are growing.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you fought for a market that phones were about to swallow.

options.label: Sell cheap-ink home photo printers. It keeps your printing know-how and your people at work.
options.outcome: In February 2007 Kodak shows its new EasyShare printers, with ink it says cuts the cost of a photo print by up to half. They go on sale in March, but they never become the big new business Kodak needs.
options.why: Cheaper ink was a clever offer for a shrinking habit. You bet on people printing photos at home just as they started keeping them on screens.
options.better: Use Kodak's know-how in chemistry and materials to enter new markets that are growing, as Fujifilm did.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you bet on home printing, a habit that was fading.

options.label: Cut film hard and move your chemists into healthcare and materials. Thousands of film jobs go.
options.outcome: You cut costs hard in film, then send your chemists into medical imaging, special films and materials. It is slow and painful, but new businesses start to replace what film used to earn.
options.why: You asked what Kodak was really good at, chemistry and materials, instead of what it used to sell. Your rival Fujifilm made the same kind of move and survived, because skills can travel to new markets even when products can't.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you defined Kodak by what it was good at, not by what it used to sell.

text.text: By 2012, Kodak is a materials and imaging company, and its photo-sharing site is where millions of families keep their pictures. Film is a small corner of the business. You changed Kodak before anyone else could.
By 2012, Kodak is a digital imaging and materials company, and film is a small, profitable corner of the business. You changed Kodak before anyone else could.

Kodak is much smaller, but it never goes bankrupt. Your photo site keeps the name in people's lives while new businesses slowly take film's place. A few earlier moves could have made Kodak a leader of the digital age.
Kodak is much smaller, but it never goes bankrupt. You fixed enough, late enough, to keep the lights on. A few earlier moves could have made Kodak a leader of the digital age.

On January 19, 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy. That April, Facebook buys Instagram, a photo-sharing app with 13 employees, for one billion dollars. The company that invented the digital camera lost the digital age.
Phones swallow the camera market, and the price war leaves Kodak with no money for anything new. Film fades, and Kodak goes bankrupt, beaten by the digital age it helped to start.
Film fades, and nothing you built is big enough to take its place. Kodak runs out of money and goes bankrupt. The company that invented the digital camera is beaten by the digital age.

fired.title: The board fires you
fired.text: The board has seen enough. After three costly calls, it gives your job to someone else, who takes over a company that is falling behind, with the clock still ticking.

realHistory: Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975, but its leaders were not convinced. It studied digital slowly after Sony's 1981 Mavica, used Ofoto to sell prints, and bet on home inkjet printers in 2007. It filed for bankruptcy on January 19, 2012 and emerged in 2013 as a much smaller company. Fujifilm, facing the same collapse, moved into healthcare, cosmetics and materials, and survived.
